newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST-S.Africa rand set to weaken slowly in '97.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-S.Africa rand set to weaken slowly in '97.

text.p: The South African rand is set to depreciate only gradually in line with inflation differentials for the rest of the year, according to results of the latest Reuters quarterly economic poll released on Thursday.
The survey of economists shows the rand is expected to end the first quarter of at 4.45 against the dollar, before gradually weakening to 4.73 by year-end.
By the end of 1998, it is expected to have weakened to 5.01 against the dollar.
Sandra Gordon, economist at Syfrets in Cape Town, said that inflation differentials of seven to eight percent should allow for continued rand stability in real terms.
"Also with privatisation going ahead I think that will offer substantial capital inflows to more than offset any outflow in terms of the lifting of exchange controls," she said.

Finance Minister Trevor Manuel announced the removal of a batch of exchange controls in his budget last week, including higher travel allowances and allowing residents to hold foreign exchange accounts, which are expected to lead to capital outflows once implemented on July 1.
Gordon noted that a more stable balance of payments situation over the next two years also pointed to currency stability.

"With the current account deficit narrowing...the whole balance payments situation will be a lot more comfortable for the next two years. That will feed through into greater stability in the currency," she said.
Nedcor chief economist Dennis Dykes said that while he also expected rand stability over the next six months, the currency could weaken at a faster pace in the latter half of 1997 into 1998.

"Structural factors, such as labour market inflexibility and tariff refoms which put a lot of pressure on exporters and import substituters, suggest that the rand should depreciate at a quicker pace in 1998," he said.
BOE NatWest chief economist Nick Barnardt felt, however, that the currency needed to depreciate by around 10 percent during the year to improve the country's growth prospects.

"The economy needs export-driven growth which the rand's movement to 4.70 last year promised to give us. A lot of that has been diluted by the sharp appreciation of the rand in the last two or three months," he said.
The rand has strengthened from around 4.70 at the beginning of this year to just below 4.40 earlier this month. On Thursday it was trading at around 4.43 against the dollar.
"If we stay at 4.40 for too long a significant part of that export boost will be diluted to a greater extent than we can really afford."
Barnardt said factors which could weigh on the rand included the impact of exchange control relaxation, the unwinding of Reserve Bank's forward book and low gold and foreign reserves.

"In fact, if we want to get three or four percent growth next year, which is politically very sensitive, we will have to go 10 percent weaker from our present level before the end of the year if we want to get a decent further boost to export growth next year."
